parts.problem_md:
Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid.

Describe the structure and bonding of a benzene molecule, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. In your answer, refer to:

- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- the bond angles within the ring
- how the *σ* and *π* bonds are formed.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structure and bonding of a benzene molecule can be described as:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The molecule is planar (or a flat hexagon)
> **AND**
> the bond angle is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bonds are formed by the head-on (or end-on) overlap of (sp<sup>2</sup>) orbitals **[1 mark]**
> - The π bonds (or delocalised system) are formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals (creating electron density above and below the plane of the ring) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When describing benzene, avoid drawing or implying **alternating double bonds**. Examiners are looking for the idea of a **delocalised π system** spread over all six carbon atoms, not localised C=C bonds.
> 
> A good way to check your answer is to mention **both** the planar structure **and** the π electron cloud above and below the ring. Together, these explain benzene’s unusual stability compared with alkenes.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid.

i) Construct an equation to show the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) Name and draw the fully labelled mechanism for the formation of nitrobenzene.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation to show the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the formation of nitrobenzene is:

![Benzene ring undergoes nitration with NO2+, forms an intermediate with NO2 and H+, resulting in nitrobenzene and hydrogen ion](assets/001-benzene-ring-undergoes-nitration-with-no2-forms-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct name of mechanism: electrophilic substitution
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the delocalised π-system of the benzene ring to the NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion (arrow must start from the ring circle and point to the N atom or + charge)
> 
> 1 mark for correct structure of the intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon **AND** positive charge clearly inside the horseshoe/ring system **AND** H and NO<sub>2</sub> attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−H bond back into the ring to restore delocalisation, showing loss of H<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In nitration mechanisms, the most common lost marks are due to curly arrows starting in the wrong place. Always start the arrow from the benzene ring circle or a C−C bond, never from a carbon atom itself.
> 
> In the intermediate, check that only one carbon is sp<sup>3</sup>, with both H and NO<sub>2</sub> attached, and that the positive charge is inside the ring, not on the NO<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> When the final arrow is drawn, it must clearly show re-formation of the delocalised π system and the loss of H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
i) State the relative order of increasing acidity for ethanol, phenol, and ethanoic acid.

[1]

ii) Identify the electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion.

[1]

iii) Describe the distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of increasing acidity is:
> 
> - Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion is:
> 
> - Positive inductive effect
> **OR**
> +*I* effect
> **OR**
> Electron-donating effect **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases is:
> 
> - Charge is spread equally over both oxygen atoms
> **OR**
> The p-orbital on the carbon atom overlaps with the p-orbitals on both oxygen atoms
> **OR**
> The negative charge / π-electrons are delocalised over the COO<sup>−</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing acid strengths, always think in terms of **conjugate base stability**. The strongest acid forms the **most stable conjugate base**.
> 
> Look for features that stabilise negative charge, such as **delocalisation** and the presence of **electronegative atoms**, and avoid explanations based only on acidity strength or pH without reference to molecular structure.

parts.problem_md: Predict the major product formed when phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The major product is:
> 
> - 4-nitrophenol
> **OR**
> 2-nitrophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at room temperature to give a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol. The -OH group activates the benzene ring and directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions.
> 
> Although 4-nitrophenol is usually formed in greater proportion due to reduced steric hindrance, both products are expected and credited at this level in line with the specification.

parts.problem_md:
Benzene can be converted into 3-chlorobenzoic acid in a multi-step synthesis.

Suggest a **three-step** synthetic route for this conversion. In your answer, identify the reagents and conditions for each step and draw the structures of the intermediate compounds formed.
parts.solution_md:
One suitable three-step synthetic route for the conversion of benzene into 3-chlorobenzoic acid is:

**Step 1** — Friedel-Crafts alkylation to give methylbenzene:

![Chemical structure of methylbenzene (toluene), showing a hexagonal benzene ring with a circle inside and a CH3 group attached](assets/002-chemical-structure-of-methylbenzene-toluene-show.png)

Reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl (or CH<sub>3</sub>Br) with AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or FeBr<sub>3</sub>) catalyst

**Step 2** — Oxidation of the methyl side chain to give benzoic acid:

![Chemical structure of benzoic acid, showing a hexagonal benzene ring connected to a COOH group](assets/003-chemical-structure-of-benzoic-acid-showing-a-hex.png)

Reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then acidify

**Step 3** — Electrophilic chlorination of the ring to give 3-chlorobenzoic acid:

Reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> with AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or FeCl<sub>3</sub>) catalyst

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for step 1 reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl / CH<sub>3</sub>Br **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeBr<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of methylbenzene (toluene)
> 
> 1 mark for step 2 reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat, then acidify
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of benzoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for step 3 reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeCl<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of the steps matters. If chlorination is done while the ring has a −CH<sub>3</sub> group, the methyl group directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions.
> 
> Oxidising the side chain first gives −COOH, which is a meta-director, so chlorination then gives the 3-chloro product.

parts.problem_md:
The nitration of benzene forms the basis for the synthesis of dyes and explosives.

i) Construct an equation for the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) State which reactant is acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and justify your answer.

[1]

iii) Identify the conjugate acid in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reactant acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and the justification are:
> 
> - Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> It accepts a proton from sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is not accepted as the Brønsted-Lowry base.
> 
> iii) The conjugate acids in the reaction are:
> 
> - H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **AND**
> NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> accepts H<sup>+</sup> from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, so HNO<sub>3</sub> is the base.
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates the proton, making it the acid.
> 
> The intermediate H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> decomposes immediately to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. Both are conjugate acids because each formed by gaining H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **B** is produced in two steps as outlined in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction scheme showing benzene undergoing Friedel-Crafts acylation in step 1 to form compound A (phenyl propan-1-one), then reduction in step 2 to form compound B](assets/004-reaction-scheme-showing-benzene-undergoing-fried.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents and conditions required for the production of compound **A** shown in Fig. 1.1.

[2]

ii) Describe the mechanism for step **1**. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents required for the production of compound A are:
> 
> - AlCl<sub>3</sub> / aluminium chloride **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl / propanoyl chloride **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for step 1 is:

![Friedel-Crafts acylation mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C+ of the acylium ion, the carbocation intermediate with horseshoe partial delocalisation and positive charge, and a curly arrow from the C–H bond restoring the ring with loss of H+](assets/005-friedel-crafts-acylation-mechanism-showing-a-cur.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the π system of the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the acylium ion (arrow must start from the ring, not inside it)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate: horseshoe opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, positive charge inside the ring, with the propanoyl group and H attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring, restoring the delocalised π system, with H<sup>+</sup> shown as lost

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acylium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) is generated when propanoyl chloride reacts with AlCl<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>
> 
> All electrophilic substitution mechanisms follow the same pattern. The most common errors are starting the first arrow from inside the ring, misplacing the positive charge in the intermediate, and omitting H<sup>+</sup> in the final step.

**Extract:**

i) The reagents required for the production of compound A are:

- CH~3~CH~2~COCl / propanoyl chloride

The acylium ion (CH~3~CH~2~CO^+^) is generated when propanoyl chloride reacts with AlCl~3~:

CH~3~CH~2~COCl + AlCl~3~ → CH~3~CH~2~CO^+^ + AlCl~4~^–^

Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for the structure of the catalyst once the electrophile has been generated in part **(b)**.
parts.solution_md:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the catalyst AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the AlCl~4~^–^ ion showing four Cl atoms bonded to a central Al atom with lone pairs on each Cl and an overall negative charge](assets/006-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-alcl-4-ion-showing-.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonds between Al and all four Cl atoms
> 
> 1 mark for the correct number of electron pairs around each Cl atom (3 lone pairs + 1 bonding pair per Cl)

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> has only 6 electrons around aluminium, making it electron-deficient. When it accepts Cl<sup>–</sup> from the acyl chloride, aluminium achieves a full octet in the tetrahedral AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> ion.

parts.problem_md: Explain why benzene can generally only undergo substitution reactions.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because:
> 
> - Addition requires breaking the delocalised π system to form new bonds **[1 mark]**
> - Breaking the delocalised π system requires significant energy input **[1 mark]**
> - The C–H bond at the ring is not part of the delocalised π system **[1 mark]**
> - Substituting H leaves the delocalised π system intact **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene's delocalised π system gives it extra stability. Addition would permanently destroy this, which is energetically unfavourable. Substitution replaces only the H atom (not part of the π system), so the ring's full delocalisation is restored after reaction.

parts.problem_md:
Methylbenzene can undergo different reactions to form the products shown in Fig. 4.1.

![Reaction scheme showing methylbenzene undergoing two different bromination reactions: side-chain free radical substitution (reaction 1) and ring electrophilic substitution (reaction 2) (Fig. 4.1)](assets/007-reaction-scheme-showing-methylbenzene-undergoing.png)

**Fig. 4.1**

State the reagents and conditions for these two reactions.

reaction 1 ........................................................................................

reaction 2 ........................................................................................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reaction 1 reagents and conditions:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> UV light **[1 mark]**
> 
> Reaction 2 reagents and conditions:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> AlBr<sub>3</sub> / FeBr<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Aqueous Br<sub>2</sub> is not accepted for reaction 2.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 1 is free radical substitution at the side chain (−CH<sub>3</sub>). UV light generates Br• radicals, so no catalyst is required.
> 
> Reaction 2 is electrophilic aromatic substitution at the ring. A halogen carrier catalyst (AlBr<sub>3</sub> or FeBr<sub>3</sub>) is required to generate the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile. The Br<sub>2</sub> must be pure (neat) as aqueous Br<sub>2</sub> will not react with the benzene ring.

![Structural diagram of benzene with a single side carbon bonded to hydrogen and two bromine atoms, C6H5CHBr2](assets/008-structural-diagram-of-benzene-with-a-single-side.png)

**OR**

![Structural diagram of benzene with a single side carbon bonded to three bromine atoms, C6H5CBr3](assets/009-structural-diagram-of-benzene-with-a-single-side.png)

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Methylbenzene can undergo different reactions to form the products shown in Fig. 4.1.

Reaction scheme showing methylbenzene undergoing two different bromination reactions: side-chain free radical substitution (reaction 1) and ring electrophilic substitution (reaction 2) (Fig. 4.1)

Reaction 2 reagents and conditions:
- Br2
AND
AlBr3 / FeBr3

Reaction 2 is electrophilic aromatic substitution at the ring. A halogen carrier catalyst (AlBr3 or FeBr3) is required to generate the Br+ electrophile.

Describe the mechanism for reaction 2. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.
parts.solution_md:
The mechanism for reaction 2 (electrophilic aromatic substitution) is:

![Electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism of methylbenzene bromination showing curly arrow attack on ring from Br+, arenium ion intermediate with horseshoe delocalisation, and H+ elimination to restore aromaticity](assets/010-electrophilic-aromatic-substitution-mechanism-of.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the benzene π system to the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium ion intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation extending over more than half of the ring but not past carbons 2 and 6; positive charge shown on ring; H shown at the substitution position
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−H bond to the positive charge on the ring **AND** benzene ring restored in product **AND** H<sup>+</sup> shown as leaving

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors in electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanisms:
> 
> - Forgetting to show the H atom at the ring carbon being substituted
> - Drawing the horseshoe delocalisation incorrectly. It must extend over more than half the ring but must not include the carbon bearing the incoming group
> - Omitting H<sup>+</sup> as the eliminated species in the final step
> - Misplacing the positive charge on the arenium ion intermediate

Nitrobenzene reacts in the same conditions as reaction **2** in part **(a)**. Draw and name the product of this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
The product of bromination of nitrobenzene under Friedel-Crafts conditions is:

3-bromonitrobenzene :

![Structural formula of 3-bromonitrobenzene showing NO2 group at position 1 and Br at position 3](assets/011-structural-formula-of-3-bromonitrobenzene-showin.jpeg)

**OR**

3,5-dibromonitrobenzene:

![Structural formula of 3,5-dibromonitrobenzene showing NO2 group at position 1 and Br at positions 3 and 5](assets/012-structural-formula-of-3-5-dibromonitrobenzene-sh.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct structure of 3-bromonitrobenzene **OR **3,5-dibromonitrobenzene
> 
> 1 mark for correct name of 3-bromonitrobenzene **OR **3,5-dibromonitrobenzene
> 
> The name must correspond to the structure given

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitro group (−NO<sub>2</sub>) is an electron-withdrawing substituent. It removes electron density from the benzene ring, deactivating it towards electrophilic substitution and directing the electrophile to the meta positions (3 and 5). This is the opposite effect to electron-donating groups (such as alkyl groups), which direct to ortho and para positions.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 2.1 shows the formation of a ketone followed by an alcohol.

![Reaction scheme showing benzene converted to a ketone via Friedel-Crafts acylation (step 1), then to a secondary alcohol via reduction (step 2) (Fig. 2.1)](assets/013-reaction-scheme-showing-benzene-converted-to-a-k.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Describe the mechanism to show the formation of the catalyst responsible for step **1**. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.
parts.solution_md:
The mechanism for the formation of the catalyst in step 1 is:

![Mechanism for formation of the acylium ion electrophile from butanoyl chloride and AlCl3, showing curly arrows for C−Cl bond breaking and Cl lone pair donating to AlCl3](assets/014-mechanism-for-formation-of-the-acylium-ion-elect.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−Cl bond to the Cl atom
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from one of the Cl lone pairs to the AlCl<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The goal is to generate the acylium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) electrophile. The overall equation is:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>
> 
> Use this equation as a guide for the curly arrows: the C−Cl bond in the acyl chloride must break (Cl leaves to form AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>), and the Cl uses a lone pair to bond to AlCl<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 2.1 shows the formation of a ketone followed by an alcohol.

Fig. 2.1

Describe the mechanism for the formation of the ketone, including the regeneration of the catalyst. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.
parts.solution_md:
The mechanism for the formation of the ketone is:

![Electrophilic substitution mechanism for Friedel-Crafts acylation showing acylium ion attack on benzene ring, arenium ion intermediate, and regeneration of AlCl3 catalyst](assets/015-electrophilic-substitution-mechanism-for-friedel.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the acylium ion (the + must be on the carbon of the acylium group)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium ion intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation extending over more than half of the ring but not past carbons 2 and 6; positive charge on ring; acylium group and H shown at the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−H bond back to the ring to restore delocalisation
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from an Al−Cl bond in AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> to the Cl atom (showing Cl<sup>−</sup> leaving)
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the Cl<sup>−</sup> to the H atom on the ring carbon, showing H<sup>+</sup> removal and regeneration of AlCl<sub>3</sub> **AND** HCl shown as a product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors in Friedel-Crafts acylation mechanisms:
> 
> - The first arrow must start touching the ring, not start inside it
> - The horseshoe in the intermediate must cover more than half the ring, with the gap at the carbon bearing the acylium group
> - The positive charge in the intermediate must be on the ring carbon (not on the acylium group)
> - In the final step, AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> acts as a Brønsted base, removing H<sup>+</sup> from the ring to regenerate AlCl<sub>3</sub> and form HCl

Reaction scheme showing benzene converted to a ketone via Friedel-Crafts acylation (step 1), then to a secondary alcohol via reduction (step 2) (Fig. 2.1)

State the reagents required for step **2**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents required for step 2 are:
> 
> - NaBH<sub>4</sub> (sodium borohydride / sodium tetrahydridoborate) **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr<sub>3</sub>, and bromoethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br, to form ethylbenzene.

Construct an equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + AlBr<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The aluminium bromide acts as a Lewis acid, accepting a bromide ion from bromoethane to generate the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> carbocation electrophile and the AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> ion.
> 
> Always ensure the halogen in the catalyst matches the halogenoalkane: AlBr<sub>3</sub> with bromoalkanes, AlCl<sub>3</sub> with chloroalkanes.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr~3~, and bromoethane, CH~3~CH~2~Br, to form ethylbenzene.

State the name of the mechanism for the formation of ethylbenzene from benzene and aluminium bromide.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the mechanism for this reaction is:

> **[exam-tip]**
> The product from part (a) is phenyl methyl ketone (acetophenone). Reduction of a ketone with NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives a secondary alcohol. The [H] notation represents the equivalent of one hydrogen atom from the reducing agent.

parts.problem_md: Explain why Friedel-Crafts acylation gives a mono-substituted product, while Friedel-Crafts alkylation may give a mixture of poly-substituted products.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Friedel-Crafts acylation gives only a mono-substituted product because:
> 
> - The acyl product contains an electron-withdrawing –COR group, which deactivates the benzene ring towards further electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - In alkylation, the product contains an electron-donating alkyl group, which activates the ring and allows further substitution to occur (polyalkylation) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acyl group withdraws electron density from the ring through the C=O bond, making the ring less reactive towards electrophiles. An alkyl group donates electron density into the ring by the inductive effect, increasing reactivity and making poly-substitution more likely.
> 
> This is a key practical advantage of acylation: it always gives a single, predictable mono-substituted product.

parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The aluminium chloride catalyst reforms because:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> is produced during electrophilic substitution when the benzene ring is restored **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

The H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring in the final step then reacts with AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> to regenerate AlCl<sub>3</sub> and release HCl. The catalyst is therefore reformed and can participate in further reaction cycles.

parts.problem_md: State the type of reaction that benzene will typically undergo.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene typically undergoes:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition because substitution restores the delocalised π system. Addition would permanently break the ring's extra stability.
> 
> The three types of substitution to know are: free radical (alkanes + halogens), electrophilic (benzene ring reactions), and nucleophilic (halogenoalkanes + nucleophiles).

parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ethyl-2-nitrobenzene is formed rather than ethyl-3-nitrobenzene because:
> 
> - The ethyl group is 2,4-directing (ortho/para-directing) **[1 mark]**

> Alkyl groups are electron-donating substituents. parts.problem_md: State the name of the mechanism that benzene will undergo if reacted with bromine in the presence of a halogen carrier to form bromobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br.

**Extract:**

Construct an equation to show how the halogen carrier generates the Br<sup>+</sup> ion in order to allow the reaction in part **(a)** to occur.
parts.solution_md:
An equation showing the generation of the Br<sup>+</sup> ion is:

AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**OR**

FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants: AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> or FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for correct products: AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup> or FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The halogen carrier acts as a Lewis acid, accepting one bromine atom from Br<sub>2</sub> to generate the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile. AlBr<sub>3</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> are equally acceptable.
> 
> The catalyst is regenerated at the end when the complex ion reacts with the H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring:
